captions.text: In 1880, a famous scientist wrote a book about how plants move.
Charles Darwin and his son Francis watched tiny grass seedlings near a window.
Light came from one side. In a few hours, the seedlings bowed toward it.
He covered some tips with tiny caps. Those seedlings hardly bent at all!
Today, seedlings on sunny windowsills still lean toward the light.
But how can we be sure they're reaching for the light?

words: When a plant grows toward or away from light. "Photo" means light and "tropism" means turning.
Something in the environment that causes a living thing to react.

parts.title: Plants Can't Walk, But They Can Grow
parts.html:
When light shines from one side, a plant can't pick up its roots and walk toward it. But it can slowly grow in that direction.

This is called phototropism. "Photo" means light. The stem and leaves bend toward the light. It happens over hours and days, too slowly to see while you watch.

parts.title: Light Is the Stimulus
parts.html:
A stimulus is something in the environment that causes a reaction. For a plant near a window, light is the stimulus.

The plant's response is to bend toward the light. The plant doesn't decide to do this. Its stem grows a little longer on the shady side, so the stem bends toward the bright side.

Roots are different. They grow down into the soil, because they respond to gravity, not light.

parts.title: Evidence in the Data
parts.html:
Scientists observe a plant over several days to find its growth pattern. One day of data doesn't show much. Four or five days together can show a clear direction.

When the stem bends more each day, always toward the same side, that's evidence. Farmers and gardeners use this. They put plants where they'll get the most sunlight.

wow.title: Darwin's tiny caps
wow.alt: An old photo of Charles Darwin in a dark hat and coat, sitting outside by a wall of ivy
wow.caption: Charles Darwin in 1881, the year after his plant book came out.
wow.html:
Darwin and his son Francis wondered which part of a seedling notices the light. So they made tiny caps out of tin foil and thin glass tubes painted black. They slipped the caps over the tips of grass seedlings.

When the tip was covered, the seedling hardly bent at all, even though the rest of it was in the light! The tip notices the light, and the bending happens lower down.
wow.insetCap: Darwin's drawing (1880): uncovered seedlings bent toward a window.

keyIdea: Phototropism is a plant's growth response to light. Light is the stimulus, and the bending stem and turning leaves are the response. Scientists find this growth pattern by observing the same plant over several days.

quiz.q: Which observation is evidence of phototropism?

options.t: The plant has roots in the soil.
options.miss: Roots and green leaves are normal plant parts. Which answer shows the plant changing direction toward the light?

options.t: The stem bends toward the window each day.
options.ok: 🌱 Yes! The stem changing direction toward the window is the response to light. That's what phototropism looks like in the data.

options.t: The plant's leaves are green.
options.miss: Roots and green leaves are normal plant parts. Which answer shows the plant changing direction toward the light?

quiz.q: Why does growing toward light help a plant survive?

options.t: It helps the plant stay warm during cold nights.
options.miss: Think about what leaves do. They make food using sunlight. So what does more light give the plant?

options.t: It helps the roots reach water faster underground.
options.miss: Think about what leaves do. They make food using sunlight. So what does more light give the plant?

options.t: Leaves need light to make food for the plant.
options.ok: ⭐ Right! Leaves use sunlight to make food. Growing toward light means the leaves can collect more of it.

items.q: The case file says: Day 1, stem straight up. Day 3, slightly toward the window. Day 5, bent toward the window. Day 7, strongly toward the window. On which day does the stem first show a response to the light?

options.t: Day 1
options.miss: On Day 1 the stem is still straight up. Look for the first day it leans.

options.t: Day 3
options.ok: Yes. On Day 3 the stem tips slightly toward the window. That's the first sign of a response.

options.t: Day 7
options.miss: By Day 7 it leans strongly, but it started leaning earlier. Look again.

items.q: In this investigation, what is the stimulus?

options.miss: The soil holds the plant up. What made the stem bend?

options.t: The bent stem
options.miss: The bent stem is the response. What caused it?

options.t: The light from the window
options.ok: Yes. The light from the window is the stimulus. The bending stem is the response.

items.q: On Day 7, someone moves the light to the left side of the plant. What will the stem most likely do over the next few days?

options.t: Slowly bend toward the left, toward the light
options.ok: Yes. The plant responds again, so the stem slowly turns toward the light on its new side.

options.t: Stay leaning right forever
options.miss: Plants keep responding to light. Where is the light now?

options.t: Fall over
options.miss: The stem won't fall. It grows toward the light. Where is the light now?
